newsitem.title: FRANCE: French doctors' strike widens, but talks planned.
newsitem.headline: French doctors' strike widens, but talks planned.

text.p: A three-week-old strike by French junior hospital doctors against government health spending curbs widened on Wednesday, prompting the government to restart talks with the protesters.
The three-week-old strike, against government plans to fine doctors if their region overshoots spending limits, has now spread to 23 of France's 26 teaching hospitals.
Two more joined the protest on Tuesday night but one voted to go back to work. Another one elected to strike from next Wednesday.
Several hundred junior doctors mounted a raucous sit-in near the Elysee presidential palace in Paris, blocking three streets until riot police removed them.
Others staged sit-ins on railway lines delaying trains at several major cities, including Bordeaux, Lyon, Lille and Montpellier, as part of the protest.
The protest has turned into a test of conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe's efforts to cut France's welfare deficit to qualify for a single European currency in 1999.

Labour and Social Affairs Minister Jacques Barrot, who refused to see the strikers on Tuesday, told reporters on Wednesday he would meet protest leaders at 6.30 p.m. (1630 GMT) but he dismissed the idea of any renegotiation of the reforms.
"I don't understand why they don't understand," Barrot said at a news conference. "We will go as far as we can with dialogue. But dialogue has a limit...We are not going to sacrifice the reforms."
Barrot said the meeting would give the doctors an opportunity to react to government proposals to include the junior doctors in upcoming plans for health care reform.
Force Ouvriere trade union leader Marc Blondel, who led a public service strike against the government plan in 1995, told France Inter radio:
"Little by little, we see that either the Juppe plan will implode or we will move to a different kind of social security with only minimal protection."

The strikers, charging the government has been deaf to their demands and is not negotiating in good faith, planned to join a protest march in Paris on Thursday by other hospital staff unhappy at cuts in hospital funding.

Unions representing specialists in private practice, who have opposed the reforms from the time they were announced in late 1995 and who have allied themselves with the junior doctors, called for a national demonstration on April 13.
But despite tough rhetoric, there were signs that the strike leaders were seeking to limit the damage.

The newspaper Liberation said they had met discreetly this week the head of the CNAM national health insurance fund, aides to Social Affairs Minister Jacques Barrot and the leader of the largest medical union, MG France, which supports the government's plans.
"We want to calm things before the April 3 strike, otherwise there is a risk this could go much farther than we want," one strike leader, Jean-Philippe Durrieu, told the daily.
The government has rejected the junior doctors' demands and accused them of promoting their own sectional interests.
The Communist-led CGT union, which represents many hospital workers, has announced it will join Thursday's march.
